map.theme: A hill-fort harbour city at dusk, where lantern-lit ramparts guard a sea gate, a crowded ledger bazaar, a lighthouse on a stone jetty, a hospital courtyard behind a rope bridge and a citadel at the summit. The palette is deep indigo, brass and lantern amber, and the mood moves from quiet vigilance at the sea gate to confident command at the citadel.

scenarios.title: Locking Down the Vidyapath College Admission Portal
scenarios.background: Vidyapath College in the fictional town of Nandipur runs its admission portal on one web server. The portal holds about 6,000 student records with entrance marks, fee receipts and scanned ID documents, and 300 staff can log in to enter marks. Passwords are currently stored as unsalted MD5 hashes. Last night someone used a stolen staff password to change the entrance marks of 40 students, and the logs show many login attempts using email and password pairs that were leaked from other websites. The portal already uses HTTPS.
constraints: The IT team is three people with a small budget
The portal must stay available during the two-week admission period
Staff and students log in from their own phones and laptops

questions.prompt: Someone used a stolen staff password to change 40 students' entrance marks in the database. Which part of the CIA triad was broken most directly?

options.text: Confidentiality, because the marks are no longer kept secret from others
Integrity, because stored data was altered without authorisation
Availability, because the portal could not serve its pages to users
Privacy, because the students' personal details appear in the changes

questions.explanation: The attacker did not just read the marks, they changed them, so the data can no longer be trusted to be accurate. Keeping data correct and unaltered by unauthorised parties is what integrity means.

why_others_wrong.a: Nothing in the incident is about the marks being disclosed; they were modified, which is a different property.
why_others_wrong.c: The portal kept working, so the data and service were still available to users.
why_others_wrong.d: Privacy is not one of the three CIA properties, and the harm here is wrong marks rather than exposed personal details.

questions.key_justification: Unauthorised modification of data is a loss of integrity.

questions.prompt: The portal stores passwords as unsalted MD5 hashes. How should passwords be stored instead?

options.text: Encrypted with AES, with the key kept in the same database as the passwords
Hashed with SHA-256 using a single fixed salt shared by every account
Hashed with a slow algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2, with a per-user salt
Kept as plain text, but readable only by the three people in the IT team

questions.explanation: Slow, memory-hard password hashes make each guess expensive, and a unique salt per user stops one precomputed table or one cracking run from working against every account at once. This is the standard way to protect passwords if the database is ever stolen.

why_others_wrong.a: Encryption is reversible, and a key stored beside the data means anyone who steals the database can decrypt every password.
why_others_wrong.b: SHA-256 is fast, so guesses are cheap, and one shared salt lets an attacker crack all accounts in a single pass.
why_others_wrong.d: Plain text means a single database leak or insider exposes every password immediately.

questions.key_justification: Passwords should be stored as slow, uniquely salted hashes, never as reversible or fast-hashed values.

questions.prompt: Attackers are trying email and password pairs leaked from other sites against student and staff logins. Which two measures most directly reduce the success of this attack?

options.text: Force all users to replace their passwords on a 30-day schedule
Require a second factor, such as an authenticator-app code, at login
Move the login form to a less obvious URL path on the website
Throttle repeated failed logins per account and per source address
Renew the HTTPS certificate with a stronger, longer encryption key

questions.explanation: A second factor means a leaked password alone is no longer enough, and throttling makes large-scale guessing slow and noisy. Together they attack both the value of the stolen password and the speed at which it can be tried.

why_others_wrong.a: A leaked pair works immediately, long before the next scheduled change, and frequent forced changes push users toward predictable variants.
why_others_wrong.c: Automated tools find the form wherever it lives, so obscurity does not stop the attack.
why_others_wrong.e: HTTPS protects traffic in transit, but the attackers are sending valid credentials over a valid connection.

questions.key_justification: Credential stuffing is blunted by a second factor and by limiting repeated attempts.

questions.prompt: Match each security measure to the type of control it is.

items.text: A firewall rule that blocks inbound traffic to ports the portal does not use
An alert that fires when one account fails 50 logins within a minute
Restoring the marks table from last night's verified backup after tampering
A login banner stating that unauthorised access will be reported to the police

questions.explanation: Blocking unused ports stops traffic before it reaches the portal, so it is preventive. An alert only reveals an attack in progress, so it is detective, and restoring from backup repairs damage after the fact, so it is corrective. A warning banner works by discouraging people from trying at all, which makes it a deterrent.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Labelling the alert as preventive: it does not stop the logins, it only tells staff about them, so it is detective. Another frequent slip is calling the restore detective, when it repairs damage rather than finding it.

questions.key_justification: Controls are classed by when and how they act: before, during or after an event, or by discouraging it.

scenarios.title: Fixing Pentest Findings at PaisaPe Co-operative Bank
scenarios.background: PaisaPe Co-operative Bank is a fictional bank serving about 80,000 customers in the town of Sundarpur through a net-banking web application. A penetration test has just reported four problems: a statement search that builds its SQL query by joining the search term into the query text, statement URLs that carry a plain account number, a payment-gateway API key that a developer committed to the private code repository three weeks ago and removed in the next commit, and several browser-facing weaknesses. A team of five developers must ship fixes within two weeks.
constraints: Downtime is allowed only on Sunday between 2 and 4 am
Five developers must ship all fixes within two weeks
Customer money and statements must not be exposed while fixes are rolled out

questions.prompt: The statement search builds its query by joining the user's search term into the SQL text. Entering ' OR '1'='1 returns every customer's transactions. What is the correct primary fix?

options.text: Use parameterised queries so the search term is always treated as data
Strip the words OR, UNION and SELECT from every incoming search term
Escape single quotes only, and keep joining the term into the query
Put the application behind a web application firewall and leave the query

questions.explanation: Parameterised queries send the SQL structure and the user's value separately, so the database never interprets the search term as code. That removes the injection at its source rather than trying to guess every harmful pattern.

why_others_wrong.b: Keyword blocklists are easy to bypass with different casing, encodings or other syntax, and they break legitimate searches.
why_others_wrong.c: Partial escaping misses other injection routes, such as numeric fields and alternate encodings, and it is easy to get wrong.
why_others_wrong.d: A firewall can reduce noise but does not remove the flaw, and a determined attacker can craft input that passes it.

questions.key_justification: SQL injection is fixed by separating code from data with parameterised queries.

questions.prompt: A logged-in customer changes accountId=10234 to accountId=10235 in the statement URL and sees a stranger's statement. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Swap sequential account numbers for long random identifiers, nothing more
Send the account number in a hidden form field rather than in the URL
Add JavaScript in the page that checks the number matches the customer
Check on the server that each requested account belongs to the customer
Log out any customer who edits the URL more than three times in a day

questions.explanation: The flaw is that the server returns an object without checking who is asking. Enforcing ownership on the server for every request fixes the real problem regardless of how identifiers look or how the request is sent.

why_others_wrong.a: Random identifiers make guessing harder but do not enforce access, so anyone who learns or leaks an identifier can still read the statement.
why_others_wrong.b: Hidden fields can be edited with browser tools or an intercepting proxy just as easily as a URL.
why_others_wrong.c: Anything checked only in the browser can be skipped by an attacker who sends requests directly.
why_others_wrong.e: Counting edits reacts after data has already been exposed and does not fix the missing authorisation check.

questions.key_justification: Broken object-level access is fixed by a server-side ownership check on every request.

questions.prompt: A payment-gateway API key was committed to the private repository three weeks ago and deleted in the next commit. Which two actions should the team take?

options.text: Revoke the exposed key with the gateway and issue a replacement
Remove the commit from the history and keep using the same key
Check the gateway logs for old-key calls from unfamiliar addresses
Base64-encode the key where it is stored in the configuration file
Wait for the next quarterly rotation since the repository is private

questions.explanation: Once a secret has been in a repository, every clone and backup may still hold it, so it must be treated as exposed and replaced. Checking the gateway's logs shows whether anyone has already used it.

why_others_wrong.b: Rewriting history does not reach copies that others have already cloned, so the old key is still compromised.
why_others_wrong.d: Base64 is an encoding that anyone can reverse, not protection.
why_others_wrong.e: Waiting leaves a possibly exposed key live for weeks, and being private does not make a repository's contents secret from every developer, clone or backup.

questions.key_justification: A secret that has been committed must be revoked and its use checked, not merely hidden.

questions.prompt: Match each web attack to the defence that addresses it most directly.

items.text: A script planted in a comment field runs in other customers' browsers
A hostile page makes a logged-in customer's browser submit a transfer
A bot tries thousands of passwords against one customer's login page
The bank's page is shown in an invisible frame to hijack customers' clicks

targets.text: Anti-forgery token that is tied to each user's session
Restriction on which sites are allowed to frame the page
Throttling and temporary lockout after repeated failures
Contextual output encoding of all user-supplied text

questions.explanation: Script injected through a comment field is stopped by encoding user text on output so it displays as text instead of running. A forged cross-site request fails when each state-changing request needs a token the attacker cannot know, repeated password guessing is slowed by throttling and lockout, and framing tricks are blocked by telling browsers which sites may frame the page.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching the hidden transfer request to output encoding because both involve a malicious page: encoding stops injected script, while a forged request is stopped by a per-session token that the attacker cannot obtain.

questions.key_justification: Each browser-side attack has a specific defence: encoding, tokens, throttling and framing restrictions.

scenarios.title: Tracing the Night Intruder at Tarkash Logistics
scenarios.background: Tarkash Logistics runs its truck-tracking system for 900 trucks from one Ubuntu server at its Rajnagar depot. At 02:20 an alert flagged 2 GB of outbound traffic. The authentication log shows 4,213 failed SSH logins as root from a single external address between 01:41 and 01:52, then 'Accepted password for root' from the same address at 01:53. The root crontab now has an entry added at 02:14 that runs a program in a hidden folder under /tmp every minute, and a new SSH public key labelled 'backup@kali' appears in root's authorized_keys file. The DNS log shows the server looking up one random-looking domain every 60 seconds. The documented 03:00 backup job and the midnight log rotation are normal.
constraints: Truck tracking must be working again by 06:00
Only two people are on call, and there is a single production server
Evidence must be kept in case the company reports the incident

questions.prompt: Evidence shows an attacker has logged in as root and left persistence behind. What should the on-call engineers do first?

options.text: Reboot the server at once so any malicious process running is cleared
Wipe the disk and reinstall the operating system from fresh media now
Isolate the server from the network and capture volatile evidence
Leave it online for a full day to observe what the attacker does next

questions.explanation: Cutting the network stops the data theft and the attacker's remote control, while capturing memory, processes and logs first preserves evidence that a reboot or reinstall would destroy. Recovery and rebuilding come after containment and evidence capture.

why_others_wrong.a: A reboot destroys volatile evidence, and the cron entry and the added SSH key would simply bring the attacker back.
why_others_wrong.b: Reinstalling at once wipes the evidence needed to learn what was taken and how the attacker got in.
why_others_wrong.d: Leaving a compromised server connected for a day gives the attacker time to steal more and to spread to other systems.

questions.key_justification: Contain the compromise and preserve evidence before eradicating or rebuilding.

questions.prompt: The server looks up one random-looking domain every 60 seconds, with identical small responses. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: Malware beaconing to its command-and-control server on a timer
Routine clock synchronisation against a public internet time server
A content delivery network warming its cache for the tracking pages
A distributed denial-of-service attack launched against the server

questions.explanation: Programs controlled by an attacker often contact their controller on a fixed timer to ask for instructions, using generated domain names that no person would type. A regular interval, an unfamiliar random name and a server that normally does not browse the web together point to beaconing.

why_others_wrong.b: Time synchronisation uses well-known time server names, not random strings, and it does not follow a strict 60-second rhythm.
why_others_wrong.c: A content network does not need the origin server to resolve a random name on a timer, and nothing here involves cache warming.
why_others_wrong.d: A denial-of-service attack would show a flood of inbound traffic to the server, not one outbound lookup per minute.

questions.key_justification: Regular lookups of a generated domain from a server are a classic sign of command-and-control beaconing.

questions.prompt: Which two findings most strongly show that the attacker set up a way to return after being removed?

options.text: A new root crontab entry that runs a hidden /tmp program each minute
A nightly burst of high CPU use on the server around 03:00 each day
Rotated and compressed log files created at midnight by log rotation
A new SSH public key labelled 'backup@kali' in root's authorized_keys
4,213 failed SSH login attempts from one address before the success

questions.explanation: A scheduled job that relaunches a hidden program and an extra authorised SSH key are both persistence mechanisms: each lets the attacker regain access even if the stolen password is changed. Neither belongs in the documented configuration of this server.

why_others_wrong.b: The 03:00 backup job is documented and explains the CPU use.
why_others_wrong.c: Midnight log rotation is a documented routine task.
why_others_wrong.e: The failed attempts show how the attacker got in, not how they would come back.

questions.key_justification: Persistence is shown by unexpected scheduled tasks and added credentials, not by routine jobs or the initial attack.

questions.prompt: Match each question the investigators need to answer to the log source that answers it best.

items.text: Which account logged in over SSH, from where, and was the password accepted?
Which outside domains did the server look up, and how many times each?
How many bytes left the server, and to which outside address was it sent?
Which tracking-site pages were requested, and with what status codes?

questions.explanation: The authentication log records logins and their outcome, the DNS log records name lookups, flow records summarise connections and the volume of data sent, and the web access log records page requests and response codes. Each answers its own question directly.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Using the DNS log to size the data theft: it shows which names were looked up but not how many bytes were sent, which is what flow records measure.

questions.key_justification: Each log source records a different kind of event, so the right source depends on the question.

questions.prompt: The compromise is already confirmed from the logs. Put these incident response activities in the order they should happen.

options.text: Restore the service from a known-good image and monitor it closely
Investigate how far the intrusion reached using the logs and captured evidence
Hold a blameless review and record what to change
Remove the attacker's persistence and fix the weakness that let them in
Isolate the server and disable the stolen account

questions.explanation: With the compromise already confirmed, the first job is to stop it spreading and stop the data leaving, so the server is isolated and the stolen account disabled. Responders then investigate the scope from the preserved evidence, remove the attacker's footholds and close the entry point, restore service from a known-good image, and hold the review last.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Restoring service before eradication, which puts a rebuilt server back online with the same open SSH access or a leftover foothold, so the attacker simply returns. Another slip is investigating at length before isolating a server that is still leaking data.

questions.key_justification: Once a compromise is confirmed: contain, investigate scope, eradicate, recover, then review.

scenarios.title: Balancing Safety and Security at Arogya Mandir Hospitals
scenarios.background: Arogya Mandir Hospitals is a fictional chain of three hospitals around the town of Vedpur. It has about 800 Windows endpoints protected only by free antivirus, 150 shared ward and ICU workstations, and an ICU central-monitoring server that can be patched only during a pre-announced maintenance window because the restart interrupts bedside alarms. A peer hospital was just hit by ransomware, and 3 of the last 4 security incidents here began with a phishing email opened on an endpoint. The board has approved Rs 40 lakh for security this year.
constraints: Patient care comes first, and alarms must never be interrupted outside a maintenance window
Phones are not allowed inside the ICU, and clinicians often wear gloves
Logging in must take under 10 seconds on shared workstations
The total budget is Rs 40 lakh

questions.prompt: A critical remote-code-execution flaw with a public exploit affects the ICU monitoring server, which only the ICU network can reach. Patching needs a restart that interrupts alarms, and the next maintenance window is in 6 days. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Patch immediately during the day shift and accept a short outage of alarms
Defer the patch to the next quarterly cycle because the server is off the internet
Accept the risk and skip the patch because no attacks on it have been reported
Patch in the window in 6 days; until then restrict it to the hosts that need it

questions.explanation: Interrupting live alarms is an unacceptable patient-safety risk, but leaving a critical flaw open is also unsafe. Patching in the nearest safe window and reducing exposure with network restrictions in the meantime manages both risks.

why_others_wrong.a: Interrupting bedside alarms outside an approved window puts patients at risk, which the constraints rule out.
why_others_wrong.b: Waiting months leaves a critical flaw with a public exploit open to anything that reaches the ICU network, such as an infected workstation.
why_others_wrong.c: The absence of reported attacks is not evidence of safety once a public exploit exists, and the next safe window is only 6 days away.

questions.key_justification: When patching must wait, limit exposure with compensating controls and patch at the first safe window.

questions.prompt: Doctors share ward workstations, wear gloves, may not carry phones into the ICU, and must log in within 10 seconds. Which second factor fits these constraints best?

options.text: A six-digit one-time code sent by SMS to the clinician's personal phone
Tap a hospital ID badge with a built-in NFC chip, plus a short PIN
A rotating code shown by an authenticator app on the clinician's phone
Answers to personal security questions about the clinician's first school

questions.explanation: A badge tap with a PIN is quick, works with gloves, needs no phone and is resistant to phishing because the secret never travels as a code a user can be tricked into typing. It satisfies every stated constraint.

why_others_wrong.a: SMS needs a phone, which is banned in the ICU, and it is also exposed to SIM-swap and interception.
why_others_wrong.c: An authenticator app also depends on a phone that cannot be carried into the ICU, and typing codes with gloves is slow.
why_others_wrong.d: Security questions are guessable or findable, so they are a weak extra factor and not a possession or inherence factor.

questions.key_justification: Choose the second factor that fits the operating constraints and resists phishing, here an NFC badge with PIN.

questions.prompt: EDR costs Rs 2,000 per endpoint per year, an email security gateway costs Rs 9 lakh a year, a new perimeter firewall costs Rs 35 lakh, and the current firewall is supported and passed its last audit. Which spending plan best fits the evidence?

options.text: Replace the perimeter firewall with a newer, higher-capacity model
Hire an external red team for Rs 25 lakh and defer all other spending
Buy EDR for all 800 endpoints and the email gateway, with a reserve
Print awareness posters and spend the rest on a faster internet link

questions.explanation: Most incidents start with phishing on endpoints that have only free antivirus, so endpoint detection and email filtering address the observed attack path. At about Rs 25 lakh in total, the plan fits the budget and leaves money for response needs.

why_others_wrong.a: The current firewall is supported and passed its audit, and spending Rs 35 lakh on it leaves almost nothing for the endpoints where incidents begin.
why_others_wrong.b: A red team would find weaknesses but not close the known phishing and endpoint gap, and it would use most of the budget on testing.
why_others_wrong.d: Posters and bandwidth do nothing to detect or contain malware once a phishing email has been opened.

questions.key_justification: Spend on the controls that address the demonstrated attack path, within budget.

questions.prompt: The hospital is considering moving from one flat network to separate segments with firewall rules between them. Which two statements about this change are accurate?

options.text: It limits how far an attacker can spread after one endpoint falls
It removes the need to patch the servers that sit inside a segment
It makes encrypting traffic between internal systems unnecessary
It adds rules to maintain, and a wrong rule can block a clinical system
It guarantees that ransomware can never encrypt any file in any segment

questions.explanation: Segmentation confines lateral movement, so one infected workstation cannot freely reach everything else. The cost is operational: every allowed flow must be defined and maintained, and mistakes can break systems that clinicians rely on.

why_others_wrong.b: Vulnerable servers can still be reached from inside their own segment, so patching remains necessary.
why_others_wrong.c: Traffic crossing or inside segments can still be intercepted, so encryption remains useful.
why_others_wrong.e: Ransomware can still encrypt files inside the segment it reaches, so segmentation reduces the spread but offers no guarantee.

questions.key_justification: Segmentation trades easier containment of attackers for more rules to manage, and it does not replace other controls.

scenarios.title: Pre-Launch Security Review for Tarang Pay
scenarios.background: Tarang Pay is a fictional wallet app from Kesarpur that launches in three weeks and expects 500,000 users in its first month. It has a mobile app, a REST API, a Postgres database and nightly backups in cloud object storage. A four-person team is running the final security review. They will model threats, rank findings, choose controls and set up monitoring, with Rs 4 lakh available to fix issues before launch. Three findings are open: the transfer API has no per-user rate limit (estimated 30% chance a year of a Rs 50 lakh loss, Rs 3 lakh to fix), all backups sit in a single region (5% chance a year of a Rs 2 crore loss, Rs 20 lakh to fix), and the admin dashboard shows software version banners (80% chance a year of a Rs 1 lakh loss, Rs 0.2 lakh to fix).
constraints: Launch is in three weeks and cannot slip
Only Rs 4 lakh is available for fixes before launch
The team of four must cover threat modelling, fixes and monitoring

questions.prompt: A customer may later claim they never authorised a transfer, and the system keeps no tamper-evident record of who did what. Which STRIDE category does this threat belong to?

options.text: Spoofing, where an attacker pretends to be a different legitimate user
Tampering, where data is altered in transit or at rest on the server
Denial of service, where the wallet is made unavailable to customers
Repudiation, where a user can deny an action and nothing proves it

questions.explanation: Repudiation is the threat that someone can deny having performed an action because there is no reliable evidence. Tamper-evident audit logs of who initiated each transfer are the usual answer.

why_others_wrong.a: Spoofing is about falsely taking another identity, whereas this threat is about the absence of proof of what a user did.
why_others_wrong.b: Tampering concerns changing data, and the concern here is missing evidence rather than altered data.
why_others_wrong.c: Nothing in the threat makes the wallet unavailable; the concern is a missing record.

questions.key_justification: A threat that someone can deny an action for lack of evidence is repudiation.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a risk assessment in the order the review team should do them.

options.text: Rank each risk by its likelihood and its impact
Identify the assets that the wallet needs to protect
Re-check the risks after the controls are in place
Choose how to treat each risk and implement the controls
Identify threats and weaknesses that could harm those assets

questions.explanation: A team cannot name threats before it knows what must be protected, and it cannot rank risks before the threats are known. Treatment and controls follow the ranking, and a final re-check confirms the risk has actually dropped.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Choosing controls before ranking the risks, which spends scarce effort on whatever is easiest or most familiar rather than on the biggest risks.

questions.key_justification: Risk work runs from assets to threats to ranking to treatment to re-assessment.

questions.prompt: With Rs 4 lakh to spend, which plan best reduces expected yearly loss across the rate-limit gap, the single-region backups and the version banner?

options.text: Fix the single-region backups alone, because that has the largest single loss
Fix the rate-limit gap and the banner, and accept the backup risk this year
Fix the version banner alone, because it is the most likely to be exploited
Fix nothing and launch on time, because the budget is below the cost of all three

questions.explanation: The expected yearly losses are about Rs 15 lakh for the rate-limit gap, Rs 10 lakh for the backups and Rs 0.8 lakh for the banner. Fixing the first and third costs Rs 3.2 lakh, inside the budget, and removes the most expected loss, while the Rs 20 lakh backup fix cannot be afforded this year.

why_others_wrong.a: The backup fix costs Rs 20 lakh, far above the Rs 4 lakh available, so it cannot be done.
why_others_wrong.c: The banner has the smallest expected loss, so fixing only it leaves the biggest affordable risk open.
why_others_wrong.d: The budget covers two cheap, high-value fixes, so doing nothing wastes it.

questions.key_justification: Rank findings by expected loss against cost and fix the best affordable combination.

questions.prompt: A copy of the nightly database backup could leak. Which two controls best reduce the risk that a leaked backup exposes wallet data?

options.text: Encrypt backups with a key held in a separate key-management service
Give the backup bucket a long random name so nobody can guess it
Store the decryption key beside the backups so restores are fast
Compress each backup with a password written in the shared runbook
Allow only the backup role to read the bucket, and log every access

questions.explanation: Encryption with a key kept elsewhere makes a stolen copy unreadable, and least-privilege access with logging makes theft less likely and easier to notice. The two controls cover protection of the data and control of who can reach it.

why_others_wrong.b: An unguessable name is obscurity, and the name can leak through logs, links or a misconfiguration.
why_others_wrong.c: A key stored next to the backups gives anyone who finds the backups the means to read them.
why_others_wrong.d: A password in a widely shared runbook is not a secret, and weak archive passwords are easy to crack.

questions.key_justification: Protect backups with encryption using separately held keys plus least-privilege, audited access.

questions.prompt: Match each attack in progress to the monitoring signal that would reveal it.

items.text: Credential stuffing against the wallet's customer logins
A service account silently gaining administrator rights
Ransomware encrypting files on a production server
A flood of requests meant to take the API offline

targets.text: Thousands of failed logins spread across many accounts
A sudden spike of inbound requests that are not login attempts
Many files renamed with a new extension while disk writes surge
A non-admin process unexpectedly added to the administrators group

questions.explanation: Credential stuffing produces many failed logins across accounts. Silent privilege escalation shows up as an unexpected group membership change, ransomware as mass file renames with heavy writes, and a denial-of-service flood as a surge of inbound requests that are not login attempts.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Matching the flood of requests to the failed-login signal because both involve many sources: stuffing is specifically repeated failed logins across accounts, while a flood overwhelms an endpoint without trying to authenticate.

questions.key_justification: Each attack leaves its own telemetry signature: failed logins, group changes, file activity or request volume.
